articleTitle: Interactive video further education and industry-the Scottish dimension
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Interactive Video Applications
abstract: The paper describes the 'Training Needs of Trainers' project which Glenrothes College managed as part of the Interactive Video in Industry and Further Education (IVIFE) programme; comments on the role which the IVIFE programme can play in developing the use of I/V in Scotland; discusses the barriers which have limited the uptake of I/V both in industry and colleges; and reviews the prospects for rapid growth in the use of I/V in Scotland in the next few years and comments on how this trend can be encouraged.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An overview of interactive video applications in the UK
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Interactive Video Applications
abstract: A large number of early interactive video applications were developed as teaching aids. Some computer based training programmes were developed to teach basic transactional skills to bank counter clerks. In 1987 the Department of Trade and Industry commissioned the National Interactive Video Centre to produce and market a range of videodisc courseware. The result so far is six interactive video courses that are already having a significant impact in the market places for which they were designed.<<ETX>>

articleTitle: Digital optical technology-what it can do for multi-media
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Interactive Video Applications
abstract: With the advent of mass storage on compact disc one is seeing the first generation of digital multi-media systems. It is hard to explain to someone a multi-media application on CDROM-XA/CD-I without them actually experiencing it. The nearest approximation is to imagine a TV program that encourages one to explore the topic, or just sit back and listen depending on one's mood. A program can be as complicated as an encyclopedia with pictures and music or as simple a computer game with a video introduction. The whole application program is encoded onto a standard 12 cm compact disc of 650 Mbytes capacity, which can contain natural still pictures, motion video, cartoon animation, graphics, text, music, and speech in any order or combination.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Interactive Video Applications
abstract: Multimedia raises important issues on the design and programming of multimedia information structures. Methodologies and tools need careful consideration in any multimedia project as the successful applications are the result of complicated trade-offs in combining the enabling technologies, various information formats and different user requirements. Multimedia applications in technology-based training, education, point-of-sale, point-of-information, documentation and in the business network are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
